fuller.text: This short essay by Paul Graham asks why talk about politics and religion turns so uniquely useless. He starts from a pattern he sees online: any mention of religion on a forum tends to turn into a religious argument. That does not happen with topics like Javascript or baking, where people feel they need some expertise before they post.

sentences.text: This short essay by Paul Graham asks why talk about politics and religion turns so uniquely useless.
He starts from a pattern he sees online: any mention of religion on a forum tends to turn into a religious argument.
That does not happen with topics like Javascript or baking, where people feel they need some expertise before they post.

fuller.text: He first tests one explanation: these topics have no definite answers, so no opinion can be proven wrong. He rejects it, because precise political questions, like what a new policy will cost, go just as badly as vague ones. His answer is that these topics become part of people's identity, meaning their sense of who they are. People cannot argue usefully about something that is part of their identity, because they are taking sides by definition.

He rejects it, because precise political questions, like what a new policy will cost, go just as badly as vague ones.
His answer is that these topics become part of people's identity, meaning their sense of who they are.
People cannot argue usefully about something that is part of their identity, because they are taking sides by definition.

fuller.text: He backs this with examples showing that the people, not the topic, are what matters. A battle involving the speakers' own countries turns political, but a Bronze Age battle probably would not, since no one knows which side to be on. Programming languages spark "religious wars" because coders see themselves as X or Y programmers, yet languages can still be better or worse designed. Even Ford versus Chevy trucks may be unsafe to discuss with some people, while politics could work with others.

fuller.text: Graham says the theory, if right, matters beyond avoiding fights: it shows how to have better ideas. If people cannot think clearly about what is in their identity, the best plan is to let as few things in as possible. He allows one possible exception: calling yourself a scientist commits you only to following the evidence, not to any belief. His conclusion is that the more labels you have for yourself, the dumber they make you.

So the trouble comes from the people, not the topic itself.
